x: Private and offline. Everything runs locally on your CPU. Nothing you ask leaves your machine, and after installing it needs no network. Small and fast. About 1 GB, no GPU. About 2 seconds an answer once loaded, and the installer offers to keep it loaded for you. Checks its own work. Every command is checked against the man pages and tldr, and whatever it cannot confirm is marked unverified. Right on your prompt. Type what you want, press Ctrl+G, and the line becomes the command, ready to edit. Nothing runs until you press Enter. Keeps your restrictions. “Without lsof”, “don't use sudo”: it answers with something else. A vague request gets a question back, not a guess. Never runs a command for you. It suggests; you decide. Anything that deletes, overwrites or formats carries a warning. Forgot the command? Just ask.

Linux on x86_64 or ARM64 (ARMv8-A: Raspberry Pi 4 and 5, ARM servers). glibc 2.28 or newer: Debian 10, Ubuntu 18.10, Fedora, RHEL 8, Arch, openSUSE and later. Alpine and other musl systems are not supported. About 1.1 GB of disk and 1.3 GB of free memory while answering. Nothing else: no Python, no compiler, no GPU. After installing, no network.

"this CPU lacks SSE4.2" or "glibc ... is too old": the machine is older than lxask supports. "this system uses musl libc": Alpine. Use a Debian or Ubuntu container instead. "checksum mismatch": the download was damaged. Run the installer again. Slow answers: about 7 seconds on a recent laptop is normal. lxask --serve brings it to about 2. On a small ARM board, expect several times that. Out of memory: lxask needs about 1.3 GB free. Close other programs, or stop a lxask --serve you no longer need with lxask --stop.
sh lxask "what you want to do" Say what you want, the way you would ask a colleague. Name the files, sizes, ages and ports you mean: lxask checks that they appear in the command.

$ lxask "delete all .tmp files in this folder" $ find . -name '*.tmp' -exec rm {} \; find Find files or directories under a directory tree, recursively -name Base of file name (the path with the leading directories removed) matches shell pattern pattern -exec Execute command; true if 0 status is returned rm Remove files or directories warning: deletes every file the find expression matches The line starting with $ is the command. lxask never runs it. Below it, each program and option, as the documentation describes it. Where the documentation says nothing, nothing is printed: an explanation can be incomplete, but it is not invented. warning: marks commands that delete, overwrite or reformat. unverified: marks what lxask could not confirm. Treat that command with more care: $ top -b -n 1 -l 1 -o %MEM | grep -v top unverified: top: -l is not a documented option closest documented example: ps --sort size Common unverified lines: line means top: -l is not a documented option the option is not in the program's manual systemctl: inspect is not a documented command no such subcommand in the manual foo: not a known Linux command no manual or tldr page knows the program pbcopy: not a Linux command a macOS or BSD command the request says '.log'; the command does not have it a detail you named is missing the request says without lsof; the command uses it it used a program you ruled out lxask has already tried up to three answers before showing one with such a line.

$ lxask "find the busiest process, see what files it has open, and stop it gracefully" 1. Find the process with the highest reported CPU usage $ ps -eo pid,comm,%cpu --sort=-%cpu | head -n 2 ... 2. List the files open by the selected process $ lsof -p PID ... 3. Send SIGTERM to the selected process $ kill -TERM PID Each part becomes its own step, answered on its own. Words in capitals like PID are for you to fill in from the step before. A note: at the end says if something you asked for is in none of the commands.

Say "without X", "don't use X", "instead of X" or "X isn't installed": $ lxask "which process listens on port 8080, without lsof" $ ss -ltnp 'sport = :8080' These requests, and requests about proxies, are answered with a version of the model trained for them (how it works).

A request too vague for one command gets a question instead of a guess, and exit status 3: $ lxask "add a proxy" "add a proxy" can mean several things. Which one? Ask again naming it, e.g.: this shell session lxask "set an http proxy for this shell session" the whole system lxask "set an http proxy system-wide for all users" Git lxask "set a proxy for git" APT lxask "set a proxy for apt" ... So far this covers proxies only.

Add one line to your shell's startup file: sh eval "$(lxask --shell-init bash)" # in ~/.bashrc eval "$(lxask --shell-init zsh)" # or in ~/.zshrc Then type what you want to do at the prompt, as plain words, and press Ctrl+G: $ count the lines in data.txt <- you type this, then Ctrl+G $ wc -l data.txt <- the line is now the command The command waits on your prompt, to edit or run with Enter; nothing runs by itself. What lxask says about it (unverified:, warning:) is printed above the prompt. A request with several steps becomes one line joined by &&. When lxask asks back or answers about itself, your line stays as you typed it. With lxask --serve running, Ctrl+G answers in about 2 seconds. To use another key, bind the widget yourself: bind -x '"\C-x\C-l": __lxask_widget' (bash) or bindkey '^X^L' __lxask_widget (zsh).

Most of an answer's time on a CPU goes into loading the model. The installer asks whether to keep lxask loaded between questions (recommended, and the default): On (serve = auto): your first question starts lxask in the background and is answered by it; later questions take about 2 s instead of about 7 (Accuracy and limits). It holds about 1.3 GB of memory while loaded and stops itself after 30 minutes without a question, so the next question starts it again. Off (serve = off): every question loads the model and frees it after. Change it in ~/.local/share/lxask/settings, or for one shell with LXASK_SERVE=auto or off. Only one copy is ever started: questions asked while it is starting wait for it. By hand, whatever the setting: sh lxask --serve & # loads once, then waits; stops after 30 minutes without a question lxask "show disk usage of each folder here" lxask --stop Every lxask call uses a running server when it can, and answers the same way. It listens on a socket only your user can open ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/lxask/, else ~/.local/share/lxask/run/). --idle MINUTES changes the timeout (0: never stop). To start it with your session, a systemd user unit: ini # ~/.config/systemd/user/lxask.service, then: systemctl --user enable --now lxask [Service] ExecStart=%h/.local/bin/lxask --serve --idle 0

sh lxask --bad # the last answer was wrong lxask --bad "should list directories only: ls -d */" # with a note (quote * and ?) The last answer is kept in ~/.local/share/lxask/last.json; --bad adds it, with your note, to feedback.jsonl beside it. Nothing leaves your machine by itself. To send reports to lxask's developers: sh lxask --share # the last report lxask --share 3 # the last three (up to 10) This prints exactly what would be sent (your question, lxask's commands, your note, the lxask version and model file) and a link to a new GitHub issue filled in with it. Open the link, remove anything private (the issue is public), and submit. lxask itself sends nothing; a GitHub account is needed to submit. Without a link: open an issue with the "Bad answer" template on GitHub.

Running the installer again keeps your choice; sh install.sh --serve or --no-serve changes it.

lxask looks at which package managers the machine has (apt/dpkg, dnf/yum/rpm, pacman, zypper, apk). If an answer uses another distribution's (yum on Ubuntu), that counts as a mistake and is retried. Listing and searching packages are rewritten for this machine: on Arch, apt search x becomes pacman -Ss x. A request that names a package manager ("with dnf") gets that one.

Commands that always need root (installing packages, mount, mkfs, systemctl start, useradd, ...) get sudo, unless lxask runs as root, the request is about a container, or the request says "without sudo".

The same flow as diagrams, with the components and the build: Architecture. question -> split into tasks -> for each task: retrieve -> answer -> check (another try if a check objects) -> explain -> warn Everything runs locally: a 1.5B-parameter language model and a small encoder through llama.cpp, and a SQLite index of documentation. The program is written in Rust.

A request with several parts ("find the busiest process, see its open files, stop it") is turned into separate tasks by one model call. Short single questions skip this. Each part is searched and answered on its own, because a long request searched as a whole brings back notes about the wrong commands. If the split loses a detail that decides which files are meant (an extension, a size, an age), it is tried again.

Each task is embedded with bge-small (37 MB) and matched against about 38,000 entries: the examples and summaries of tldr-pages, plus a summary for each command only a man page documents. The search first picks the four commands the task is most likely about, favouring common ones over obscure tools unless a tool is named, then takes their closest examples. These notes go into the model's prompt. Without the encoder, the search falls back to keywords (BM25).
A fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, quantized to 4 bits, writes one command line for the task, and nothing else.

The command is checked without running it: Against the documentation. The program exists, every option is documented for it, the subcommand after systemctl and its kin is real, the line parses as shell, and it is not a macOS or BSD form (top -l, sed -i '', pbcopy). Against the task. The paths, extensions, sizes, ages, counts and ports the task names must appear in the command, in any form a command can write them: 30 days is -mtime +30, -mmin +43200 or --since '30 days ago'. Against known slips. grep on a directory without -r, a reboot for "shut down", pip list for the system's packages, $HOME/... when the request never mentioned home, a command that deletes for a request that only asks to look. When a check objects, or no command came back, the model gets up to two more tries (sampled, so they differ), and the answer with the fewest objections is kept. What still fails is shown as unverified:. Slips with exactly one right fix are repaired instead: head -n 1 after ps (that is only the header) becomes head -n 2; grep on a directory gets -r; a bare crontab line is installed with crontab; a command that always needs root gets sudo; another distribution's package listing or search becomes this machine's.

"Without lsof", "don't use sudo", "instead of curl", "netstat isn't installed": a command that runs a ruled-out program is an objection, judged on what it actually runs (sudo lsof, xargs grep, find -exec rm), not on the words ("without deleting" rules out nothing). Documentation notes about that program are kept out of the prompt. Such requests, and requests about proxies, are answered with a small LoRA adapter (37 MB) applied on top of the model. It was trained on these requests and keeps restrictions much better (80% against 60%), but it is worse on everyday questions, so every other request gets the model alone. LXASK_ADAPTER=off turns it off.
Some requests mean different commands in different contexts. For those ("add a proxy" with no word on where), lxask asks which one is meant instead of guessing.
Each program and option in the command is looked up in the tldr summaries and the man pages. Where the documentation says nothing, nothing is printed.

Commands that delete, overwrite or reformat (rm -r, find -delete, dd to a device, mkfs, shred, git reset --hard) carry a warning: saying what kind of command it is. The warning does not say whether the command's filter is right; you check that.

The base model was fine-tuned on about 39,000 examples, from tldr-pages, NL2Bash and generated requests checked by the same validator. It then had a round of reinforcement learning on commands that were actually run in a sandbox, rewarded when they produced the right result. Results has every training round, including the ones that were not shipped.

lxask is one Rust program and four files: the model, its restriction adapter, a small encoder and a SQLite index of documentation. Everything runs on your machine, on the CPU. Python is used only to build those files and to measure the result, and it calls the same Rust core the program uses, so what is measured is what ships. For the reasoning behind each step in prose, see How it works; for numbers, Results.

What happens between lxask "..." and the printed command (rust/crates/lxask/src/main.rs, rust/crates/lxask-core/src/answer.rs): Two shortcuts answer without the model at all: questions about lxask itself, and requests too vague for one command ("add a proxy"). Everything else goes through the model, one call per task plus one for the split, and up to two more per task when the checks object.

crate what it is lxask the program: options, the server, feedback, settings lxask-core every rule, with no I/O: the model and the search are passed in, so it is tested without them lxask-llm the model, the adapter and the encoder, through llama.cpp lxask-py the core as the Python module lxask._core, used by src/lxask and scripts/

lxask --serve keeps everything loaded, so later questions skip the few seconds of loading. With serve = auto (the installer's default) a question that finds no server starts one in the background, detached from the terminal, and waits for it; a lock next to the socket makes sure only one is started (server::start_and_wait).

t: How the model and the index are made
x: Offline, on a machine with a GPU (a free Colab T4 or a laptop RTX card): The evaluation sets are kept out of training throughout; the execution tests run each command as an unprivileged user in a container with no network (Development).

Everything lives in ~/.local/share/lxask: the model, the adapter, the encoder, the index, last.json and your feedback.jsonl; the program is ~/.local/bin/lxask. The full list and every setting: Configuration.

Check, don't trust. A 1.5B model gets details wrong, so every command is checked against the documentation and the request, retried when a check objects, and marked unverified: when it still fails. It never runs a command. Small, local, offline. One program and about 1.1 GB of files, 1.3 GB of memory while answering, no network after installing. Route instead of retrain. The model fine-tuned on restrictions got worse on everyday questions, so it ships as an adapter used only for the requests it is better at (Results). Ask back instead of guessing when a request means different commands in different contexts. Fixed text for questions about lxask, rather than teaching the model facts about itself. One core for the program and the measurements. Training and evaluation call the same Rust code through lxask._core.

lxask usually picks the right tool and the right shape of command. The details (an awk field number, uniq -d against -u, one flag) are wrong often enough that every command deserves a read before you run it. A 1.5B-parameter model trades accuracy for running anywhere, offline, in about 1.3 GB of memory.

Every set below was kept out of training. test n result right program, everyday questions (hand-written) 150 96-99% right program, tldr examples 150 75% (50% exactly the reference command) right program, NL2Bash questions 150 80% multi-part requests: parts handled 288 91-100% command run in a sandbox does the job, generated file and text tasks 200 75% the same, hand-written tasks 46 87% restriction kept ("without lsof") 40 80% restriction kept, programs never ruled out in training 79 76% vague proxy request asked back, clear one answered in the right form 24 79% past mistakes that must not come back 7 7 of 7 "Right program" means the command uses a program a correct answer would use; it says nothing about the options. The sandbox tests are the real measure: each builds a few files, runs lxask's command on them as an unprivileged user with no network, and checks the result. To pass, the command must also exit cleanly, leave files alone when the task only asks a question, and use nothing the task ruled out. How each set is made and scored: Development. Every version's numbers: Results.

The sets above are lxask's own. For a number that can be checked against other tools, the model was also run on the public NL2SH-ALFA test set (300 shell tasks) through the InterCode-ALFA harness (icalfa 0.3.6): each answer is run in a Docker container and counts as solved only when the harness gives it a reward of exactly 1. The harness's embedding judge decides (threshold 0.75, a local embedding model; nothing hosted). Answers come from the real pipeline (retrieval, checks, retries, the 0.8 adapter) and, for comparison, from the untuned Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B the model was trained from (the stock Q4_K_M build), greedy, with no retrieval and no checks. The untuned model is run three ways, because how it is asked changes its score a lot: base, raw: a plain instruction, and only code fences stripped from its reply. This was the baseline first published here (31%). It was handicapped: 199 of its 300 replies were wrapped in backticks or started with $ , which fail when run, and 169 of those scored 0 for that reason alone. base, cleaned: the same replies with the backticks and $ removed. base, three examples: the plain instruction plus three worked examples (none from the test set) and "no backticks, no $". This is the strongest baseline and the one the README compares against. variant solved 95% CI (Wilson) lxask 187/300 (62%) 57-68% untuned base, three examples 162/300 (54%) 48-60% untuned base, cleaned 153/300 (51%) 45-57% untuned base, raw (the handicapped first run) 92/300 (31%)

Details. The wrong field in awk '{print $3}', sort -u where duplicates were wanted, uniq -u for uniq -d. Most failed sandbox tasks are like this. Placeholders. A path from the documentation (path/to/directory) can stay in the command instead of the one you named. Invented subcommands. Subcommands are checked for systemctl and its kin only; elsewhere an invented one (apt-config set) can pass unmarked. Judgement. "Which files are safe to remove" gets commands for looking, not the judgement. Heavy one-liners. Time-windowed aggregation over quoted CSV and similar are beyond a model this size. Vague requests. Asking back covers proxies only; other vague requests still get a guess. Explanations. Programs without a man page on the reference install are checked by name only, and their options are not explained.

Tuned and tested on Debian and Ubuntu. On other distributions most commands are the same (find, grep, awk, tar, ssh, systemctl, ip, ss), and package commands adapt: see Configuration. Other distribution-specific advice may still lean Debian, for example ufw where firewalld runs. No numbers have been measured on Fedora or Arch yet.

Measured with the release program (version 0.6; the adapter added in 0.8 cost about 2% more time) on a Ryzen 9 270 laptop CPU, in a 2 GB container, median of five everyday questions, including loading (when not served), retrieval, checks and explanations: time one question, lxask "..." (loads the model each time) 6.6 s one question with lxask --serve running 2.0 s multi-part request (median of ten), not served 15.6 s A multi-part request costs one model call per part plus one for the split, and up to two more per part when a check objects. Commands in the training set come from three places, and every one has passed lxask.validate: tldr-pages: the documentation's own examples. NL2Bash: human-written pairs, minus what the validator rejects. That removes the macOS commands (top -l, pbcopy, sed -i '') round 1 learned from. Generated: scripts/generate_data.py asks a language model for natural questions with commands and for multi-part requests split into self-contained steps. Single tasks come from three jobs: tasks and depth (one request per command, grounded in its tldr page and man options; depth asks again for the most used commands) and everyday (questions that never name the tool). Multi-part requests come from scenarios (1 to 4 parts) and long (4 to 6 parts). Round 3 added scenarios3, retask, constraints and fix, round 6 forbid, forbid_scenarios, contexts and forbid_twins (see results). scripts/filter_generated.py keeps an item only if every command in it passes the validator. "Passed the validator" means the program and its options exist. It does not mean the command does what the question asks. For that, the review job has a stronger model judge every task the small model wrote, and the filter drops what it rejects (about one in ten; roughly two thirds of those were plainly wrong, the rest arguable). A sample is still read by hand, and a percent or two of the remaining answers are expected to be wrong in meaning. t: The public benchmark: NL2SH-ALFA (300 tasks), the shipped model
x: The model shipped since 0.8 (round 4 with the restriction adapter) was run on the public NL2SH-ALFA test set through the InterCode-ALFA harness (icalfa 0.3.6, every answer executed in Docker, embedding judge at 0.75, local). It solves 187 of 300 (62%, 95% CI 57-68%) against 162 of 300 (54%, CI 48-60%) for the untuned Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B it was trained from when that model is given three worked examples (paired exact McNemar, p = 0.003); on the 237 tasks with no overlap with its training sources, 61% against 54% (p = 0.024). Keeping the first answer (no retries) scores the same 187 and dropping retrieved notes 186, so the checks and the retrieval show no measurable effect on this set; the difference is fine-tuning. The first published baseline (31%) was handicapped by a reply-cleanup bug and was corrected on 2026-10-23: see the correction in Accuracy and limits, which also has the full table, the difficulty breakdown, the judge's context-error caveat and why other tools' numbers on this set are not comparable.

Only the restriction tasks of exec_tasks are routed: 3 more pass (awk 'END {print NR}' without wc, awk /error/ without grep, cat > copy without cp) and 2 fewer (cat /dev/null > old.txt empties the file instead of deleting it; perl counting lines for words). Of those 745 questions one is routed (an ssh SOCKS proxy; same answer). The one changed answer (rsync -an for rsync -av on a dry run) is the question after it: switching back empties the prompt cache, and a prompt computed whole rounds slightly differently from one that reuses a cached

A list of ruled-out programs is read to its end: "without lsof, netstat, or ss" rules out all three, while "show the log without the header, and grep for ERROR" still rules out nothing but the header. A request that only asks to look ("show which files can safely be removed", "list", "check", "count") answered with a command that deletes (rm, rmdir, unlink, shred, find -delete) is an objection: retried, and marked if it stays. It flags 2 of 32,421 known-good pairs. "Set a proxy in .curlrc" (or .wgetrc) names a context and is no longer asked back. t: Report a bug or suggest something

Setup, building and tests: docs/development.md. The rules (checks, repairs, routing) are in rust/crates/lxask-core, and the Python training and evaluation scripts call the same code through lxask._core. Rust tests: cargo test --manifest-path rust/Cargo.toml -p lxask-core; Python tests: pytest (no model needed). A change to a rule should not change answers it is not about. Run the evaluation before and after (scripts/eval.py, see docs/development.md) and say in the pull request what moved. Keep commits small and their messages about why.

The training data written by language models is not in this repository (see NOTICE and docs/development.md). scripts/generate_data.py makes it again with your own API key; read your model provider's terms on using its output for training before you do.

t: What lxask does and does not do
x: lxask never runs the commands it suggests. It prints them; you decide whether to run them. Read every command before you do, especially ones marked warning: or unverified:. It needs no network after installing and sends nothing anywhere. lxask --share only prints a link; nothing leaves your machine unless you open it and submit the issue yourself. lxask --serve listens on a Unix socket in a directory only your user can open ($XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/lxask/) and answers only that user. The installer checks every downloaded file against the release's SHA256SUMS.

If you find a security problem (for example a way for one user to talk to another user's server, a file written where it should not be, or the installer trusting something it should not), please report it privately through GitHub's security advisory form rather than a public issue. Say what you found, how to reproduce it, and the lxask version (lxask --version). If the form is not available, open an issue that only asks for a private way to report, without the details. A dangerous command suggested by the model is a wrong answer rather than a security hole in the program: report it with lxask --bad and lxask --share, or as a "Bad answer" issue.
